title: India Is Quietly Interrogating Companies That Sent Money Abroad. The Rupee Crisis Made It Inevitable.
excerpt: The RBI and SEBI have sent at least 10 queries in three weeks to firms and family offices routing money overseas. The $250,000 LRS window is next.
body:
India's central bank and markets regulator have begun tightening scrutiny on overseas investments by companies and family offices, issuing at least 10 formal queries in the past three weeks to examine whether funds were routed abroad without a clear business purpose or tangible asset backing. Three sources with direct knowledge of the matter confirmed the move to Reuters.

The crackdown comes as the rupee has fallen to record lows near 97 per dollar, foreign investors have pulled out a record $27 billion from Indian equities this year, and oil prices have pushed past $97 per barrel on renewed hostilities in the Middle East. India's balance of payments deficit is projected to widen to $65 billion in 2026-27, nearly double last year's $35 billion.

"The scrutiny is not about curbs but about the pace of capital outflows and why and whether they are exacerbating pressure on the currency and reserves," one source said.

## What Regulators Are Looking At

The Reserve Bank of India and the Securities and Exchange Board of India are focusing on three areas: large overseas investments routed through opaque corporate structures, inflated valuations of offshore assets used to justify fund transfers, and the use of Overseas Direct Investment routes as a vehicle for private wealth management by individuals and family offices.

India's capital account is only partially open. Companies can invest abroad through the ODI route, subject to net worth-linked limits and for specified purposes. Individuals can remit up to $250,000 annually under the Liberalised Remittance Scheme for education, healthcare, and investments. The LRS has long been the primary mechanism through which upper-middle-class Indians and NRIs move money across borders.

Neither the RBI nor SEBI responded to Reuters' queries about the letters.

## The Broader Defensive Posture

The overseas investment scrutiny is one piece of a much larger effort to stem dollar outflows. In May, India raised import tariffs on gold and silver from 6 percent to 15 percent, combining a 10 percent basic customs duty with a 5 percent Agriculture Infrastructure and Development Cess. This week, it placed silver bars with 99.9 percent purity under the restricted category with immediate effect.

The government has tightened rules for duty-free gold imports for jewellery exports, capping imports at 100 kilograms per licence. Prime Minister Modi has publicly appealed to citizens to avoid unnecessary foreign travel and urged remote work to conserve fuel and reduce costly oil imports.

The RBI has also been intervening directly in currency markets, selling dollars through state-run banks almost every session since the rupee hit its record low of 96.96 in mid-May. To manage the impact on its reserves and domestic liquidity, the central bank has paired these sales with dollar-rupee buy-sell swaps, which effectively convert spot dollar sales into short-term forward positions.

## The RBI Decision on Friday

All of this is building toward Friday's monetary policy decision. A Reuters poll found that nearly 80 percent of economists expect the RBI to hold the repo rate at 5.25 percent. But a growing minority — 11 of 56 polled — forecast a 25 basis-point hike to support the currency. Interest rate swaps are pricing in nearly 100 basis points of tightening over the next 12 months.

Bank of America Securities warned that the rupee could fall to 98 per dollar by July if the energy shock continues. Asia's worst-performing currency this year, the rupee was trading at 95.70 on Wednesday.

## Why NRIs Should Pay Attention

For the Indian diaspora, the scrutiny has immediate implications. The $250,000 LRS limit — the most common route for NRIs to move money for education, property, or investment purposes — has not been changed. But the regulatory tone has shifted unmistakably. Family offices in India that manage wealth for diaspora families using ODI structures are now under the lens. Inflated offshore valuations, a common feature of some cross-border wealth transfers, are drawing specific attention.

The broader message from Delhi is clear: every dollar leaving India will be watched more closely than at any point since the 2013 currency crisis, when then-Governor Raghuram Rajan launched a series of emergency measures to shore up the rupee. RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra has already said the central bank will do "whatever is required" — but so far, the actions have lagged the rhetoric.

*Sources: Reuters, Bloomberg News, The Hindu BusinessLine*
author: Diaspora Desk
